study_identification_part.si4_title: Age-Associated Deviations of Amygdala Functional Connectivity in Youths With Psychosis Spectrum Disorders: Relevance to Psychotic Symptoms

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To create normative growth charts of amygdala functional connectivity in typically developing youths, assess age-associated deviations in youths with psychosis spectrum disorders, and explore the relationship between these disruptions and clinical symptomatology.

caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: Using the model of best /uniFB01 t for developmental changes observed for amygdala connectivity in the typically developing control group, we predicted what the expected ' normative ' amygdala connectivity value would be for the psychosis spectrum group. We then subtracted the predicted value from the actual amygdala connectivity value for each individual and took the absolute value of this score. This created an amygdala connectivity maturation deviation score...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Pearson correlations were computed between the 'amygdala connectivity maturation deviation score' and positive symptoms, corrected for multiple comparisons using FDR (q < 0.1). Post-hoc Pearson correlations were used to examine specific symptoms (grandiosity, hallucinations) and to analyze associations within specific developmental periods after regressing out covariates.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Youths with psychosis spectrum disorders exhibit a lack of normative developmental decreases in amygdala connectivity, and greater deviation from the typical trajectory of amygdala-thalamus connectivity is associated with more severe positive symptoms.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study established normative developmental charts showing age-related decreases in centromedial amygdala connectivity. Youths with psychosis spectrum disorders failed to show these normative decreases in connectivity with the striatum, thalamus, lateral prefrontal cortex, and occipital cortex. Alterations in centromedial amygdala-striatum and -occipital cortex connectivity were specific to the psychosis group. Greater deviation from the normative trajectory of centromedial amygdala-thalamus maturation was associated with increased positive symptom severity (r=0.19, q=0.05).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: 1. The clinical group data was cross-sectional, so developmental trajectories reflect group trends, not within-person change. 2. It's unclear if results are due to altered development or abnormalities from the onset of psychosis. 3. Site effects, though accounted for, might have obscured more subtle findings.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Our study was limited by the fact that cross-sectional data were available only for the psychosis spectrum group. Thus, the neurodevelopmental trajectories in psychosis spectrum disorders do not re /uniFB02 ect within-person change. Our crosssectional sample cannot de /uniFB01 nitively show whether our results are due to altered development or abnormalities due to time of onset of psychosis. ... Site effects may have obscured our ability to identify smaller developmental changes in normative amygdala connectivity developmental trajectories.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study introduced a 'amygdala connectivity maturation deviation score' (absolute difference from norm) to relate dysmaturation to symptoms. It also serves as a proof-of-principle for merging multiple 'big data' resting-state fMRI datasets to create normative growth charts.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: A key methodological feature is the creation of 'growth charts' for brain connectivity, analogous to pediatric growth charts for height/weight, to identify atypical development. The study successfully combined four datasets from two universities, scanned on the same model of scanner but with different parameters, by including 'site' as a covariate, demonstrating a method for handling multi-site data.
